summary: A note from BBN proposing three aids to improved network operation. The first reserves 7 to 8 a.m. Eastern time every Tuesday for IMP software reloads, since the network never sleeps and downtime is hard to schedule. The other items are further operational improvements.

plainLanguage.summary: The network's operators set aside one early hour each week to restart machines, so users are never surprised by a break. They also made the machines give clearer reasons and better warnings before they shut down.

subtitle: BBN reserves Tuesday mornings for IMP reloads, adds warnings before shutdowns, and reworks the IMP-to-Host messages.

tldr.problem: The ARPA Network never sleeps, so loading new IMP software without disrupting someone was hard, and the IMP-to-Host error messages were often imprecise or ambiguous.
tldr.mechanism: BBN reserves 7 A.M. to 8 A.M. eastern time every Tuesday for IMP reloads, extends the IMP-Going-Down message with a reason and timing, and revises the IMP-to-Host message types on August 14, 1972.
tldr.outcome: A network news service was also started. The unit metadata lists RFC 394 as a later update.

today: The unit metadata gives RFC 381 no formal status and lists RFC 394 as a later update. It records a 1972 operating practice and message layout for the ARPA Network.

sections.title: Scheduled Software Maintenance
sections.content:
As the network grew, BBN found it hard to slot in new software without disrupting anyone. There is always traffic between the machines at MIT and almost always traffic between the AMES TIP and IMP, since the sun never sets on the ARPA Network. So BBN reserves 7 A.M. to 8 A.M. eastern time every Tuesday for reloading IMPs. It will probably not use the period every week, but it reserves it. This is on top of the several hours a month already scheduled at each site for hardware preventative maintenance.

Emergency restarts and reloads still happen, and a restart is preceded by several minutes of warning with an IMP-Going-Down message. In every case where an IMP is shut down intentionally, a type 2 IMP-to-Host message is sent about 30 seconds before it goes down. An IMP may crash too quickly to warn anyone, but the RFC says it will never be intentionally shut down that way.
sections.plainLanguage: Every Tuesday morning at seven, the operators might briefly switch off a machine. They keep to that one time so nobody is caught by surprise.

sections.title: IMP-to-Host Messages
sections.content:
Users had long complained that IMP-to-Host error messages were not precise enough or were ambiguous. The new meanings, which include the additions proposed in RFC 312, take effect on August 14, 1972. Hosts are encouraged to update their NCPs by then; unmodified NCPs will probably keep working, but each site should check carefully.

The generalized type 2 IMP Going Down message uses bits 17 to 32. Bits 17,18 give the reason (01 scheduled hardware PM, 10 scheduled software reload, 11 emergency reload or restart), bits 19 to 22 say how soon in 5 minute units, and bits 23 to 32 say how long in 5 minute units. All bits zero means going down in 30 seconds. Hosts and the TIP should use this to remind their users.

In summary: there is now exactly one IMP-to-Host message for each regular Host-to-IMP message; types 1, 2, 7 and 9 carry extra information; type 10 is added; types 3 and 6 are discarded. Type 9 now distinguishes, for example, a message too long (more than 8095 bits) from one too slow (more than 15 seconds between first and last bit).
sections.plainLanguage: The machine used to say only that something went wrong. Now it says what went wrong and when it will switch off, so hosts can warn their users in time.

sections.title: Network News Service
sections.content: The third aid is a network news service. TIP users read the news by typing the command @NEWS. Users of other hosts can get it by ICPing to socket 15600031 (octal) at the BBN Tenex. The note ends by asking for further suggestions to improve network operation.
sections.plainLanguage: There is now a bulletin board for the network. You can read it with a short command, or by connecting to the right door number.
